Jejune means empty of substance. Think of it as the opposite of rich, deep, or nourishing — whether we're talking about ideas, writing, or a person's thinking. When you call something jejune, you are saying it falls flat because it lacks depth, maturity, or life.

The word carries two closely related meanings that often work together.
Meaning 1: Naive, Simplistic, or Intellectually Immature

This is the most common modern meaning. When someone's thinking is jejune, it means their ideas are childishly oversimplified — they treat a complicated subject as if it were simple, they overlook important nuances, or they show a lack of real-world wisdom.

For example, imagine someone arguing that all crime could be eliminated if people were just "nicer to each other." That's a jejune argument — it is innocent, shallow, and ignores the complex social, economic, and psychological forces at play. It is the kind of argument a young, inexperienced person makes before they've thought deeply about the world.

Jejune in this sense doesn't just mean "wrong." It means naively wrong — wrong in a way that reveals a lack of maturity or experience. It's slightly condescending when used this way.

The second meaning refers to something that fails to stimulate or engage. A jejune piece of writing, speech, or performance is flat, colorless, and uninteresting. It goes through the motions without spark, passion, or originality. It bores you not because it's offensive, but because it offers nothing to hold your attention or feed your mind.

Imagine reading a travel article about Paris that does nothing but list street names, opening hours, and ticket prices, with no sense of wonder, no vivid description, no personality. That article is jejune. It technically contains information, but it feels empty.

Here's the key insight: these two meanings often come packaged together, and that is what makes jejune such a precise and powerful word.

Something that is intellectually naive tends also to be dull. A simplistic argument, by its very nature, offers little to think about — so it is both shallow and boring. A flat, lifeless essay is often that way because the writer had no deep ideas to express — shallow thought produces dull writing.

This is why writers and critics love jejune — in one word, it says "this is both unsophisticated and uninteresting." It delivers a complete, two-layered dismissal.
Tone and Register: Who Uses This Word?

Jejune is a formal, literary word. You will encounter it in book reviews, literary criticism, academic essays, and high-quality journalism. It is rarely used in everyday conversation. When someone reaches for it, they usually have high intellectual standards and are expressing disappointment that something has failed to meet them.

The word has a faintly superior or snobbish quality — it is the word of a critic or a scholar, not a casual observer. If someone calls your essay "jejune," they aren't just saying it's bad; they're saying it's beneath the level of depth they expected from you.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Naive means innocently unaware or inexperienced, but it doesn't necessarily mean boring or worthless. A naive person can still be charming and interesting.
  • Boring means something fails to hold your attention, but it doesn't imply intellectual shallowness or immaturity.
  • Superficial is close, but it focuses on a lack of depth without the additional sense of dullness.
  • Jejune does all three things at once — shallow, immature in thought, and lifeless. It's a fuller, more layered insult.

1. "His political opinions were jejune — he had clearly never encountered a perspective different from his own." (naive, simplistic)
  2. "The professor's lecture was so jejune that half the class was asleep by the end." (dull, lifeless)
  3. "The novel's dialogue felt jejune, as if the author had never observed how real people actually speak to each other." (both shallow and flat)
  4. "She had outgrown her jejune idealism and replaced it with something harder but more honest." (immature, oversimplified)

If you want to remember this word forever, anchor it to this:

Jejune describes something that disappoints you by being thin — thin in thought (naive, simplistic) and thin in life (dull, flat).

Any time you encounter a piece of writing, an argument, or an idea that leaves you feeling like you were handed a cup that was supposed to be full but was practically empty — jejune is your word.
